text: Lesson 1 described Sentinel's economics as paying for what you ingest and retain, instead of hardware bought up front. This lesson is what that actually looks like in practice — the real pricing model, and the retention choices that go with it.

Sentinel's default pricing model is pay-as-you-go, billed per gigabyte of data ingested per day into the Log Analytics workspace. Every connector from the last lesson that's turned on contributes to that daily volume, which is why connector choices and pricing aren't separate conversations — turning on a high-volume source, like raw Windows Security Events from every server in a large environment, is a direct, predictable cost decision.

For organizations with large, fairly consistent daily ingestion, Microsoft offers commitment tiers — fixed daily volume levels like 100 or 200 gigabytes per day, billed at a discounted rate versus pure pay-as-you-go. Pay-as-you-go stays more flexible for unpredictable or low volume, while a commitment tier gets cheaper per gigabyte once ingestion settles into a steady, high-volume pattern.

Retention is how long ingested data stays queryable. A Sentinel-enabled workspace includes a free interactive retention window at no extra ingestion cost, letting analysts query and detect against that data normally. Keeping data queryable longer than that costs additional storage per gigabyte per month, which is why retention isn't a set-it-to-maximum-and-forget-it setting — it's a real monthly cost trade-off.

For data that must be kept for compliance far longer than anyone expects to actively query it, Sentinel supports an archive tier. Archived data is stored far more cheaply, but it isn't instantly queryable the normal way — getting back to it requires a search job or a restore operation first, which takes time and isn't meant for day-to-day detection work.

Put connectors and retention together and a real question comes into focus: is a source valuable enough for active detection to justify interactive retention, or does it mostly need to exist for compliance, where archive is the far cheaper home once it ages out of active use? That closes out this chapter's architecture — next, Chapter 2 turns to actually querying this data with KQL.
